CFA.paraphrase: Uncharted special use airspace that contains activities that would be hazardous to nonparticipating aircraft outside a controlled environment; the activities stop when an aircraft approaches.
CFA.definition: Airspace that contains activities that are a danger to non-participating aircraft when they are not in a controlled environment. They stop at once when spotter aircraft, radar or ground observers find an aircraft that approaches.
CFA.note: The FAA puts the CFA in special use airspace without regulatory status. An aeronautical chart does not show it, and it has no set dimensions. This type is not in AJP-3.3.5 Annex B. It is an airspace type of civil aviation, thus it is an `airspace_type` value, not a catalogue code.

NSA.name: National Security Area
NSA.source_text: NSAs consist of airspace of defined vertical and lateral dimensions established at locations where there is a requirement for increased security and safety of ground facilities. Pilots are requested to voluntarily avoid flying through the depicted NSA. When it is necessary to provide a greater level of security and safety, flight in NSAs may be temporarily prohibited by regulation under the provisions of 14 CFR section 99.7.
NSA.paraphrase: Airspace of defined vertical and lateral dimensions over ground facilities that need increased security and safety; pilots voluntarily avoid it, and a regulation may temporarily prohibit flight in it.
NSA.definition: Airspace of defined vertical and lateral dimensions at locations with ground facilities. At these locations, it is necessary to increase security and safety. The FAA tells pilots to avoid flight through it. A TFR can temporarily close it to flight.
NSA.note: The FAA puts the NSA in special use airspace without regulatory status. A TFR in the conditions of 14 CFR 99.7 can close it temporarily. This type is not in AJP-3.3.5 Annex B. It is an airspace type of civil aviation, thus it is an `airspace_type` value, not a catalogue code.

TFR.name: Temporary Flight Restriction
TFR.locator: Entry temporary flight restriction, page T-3
TFR.source_text: A TFR is a regulatory action issued by the FAA via the U.S. NOTAM System, under the authority of United States Code, Title 49. TFRs are issued within the sovereign airspace of the United States and its territories to restrict certain aircraft from operating within a defined area on a temporary basis to protect persons or property in the air or on the ground.
TFR.paraphrase: A regulatory action that the FAA issues by NOTAM to restrict certain aircraft from a defined area for a limited time, to protect persons or property in the air or on the ground.
TFR.definition: A regulatory action of the FAA in a NOTAM. It temporarily restricts some aircraft from operation in a defined area. Its function is the protection of persons or property in the air or on the ground.
TFR.note: Each NOTAM gives the dimensions of its TFR. The FAA puts the TFR in special activity airspace. This type is not in AJP-3.3.5 Annex B. It is an airspace type of civil aviation, thus it is an `airspace_type` value, not a catalogue code.

SFRA.name: Special Flight Rules Area

references.locator: Entry special flight rules area, page S-7

SFRA.source_text: Airspace of defined dimensions, above land areas or territorial waters, within which the flight of aircraft is subject to the rules set forth in 14 CFR part 93, unless otherwise authorized by air traffic control.
SFRA.paraphrase: Airspace of defined dimensions above land or territorial waters where flights follow the special air traffic rules of 14 CFR part 93 unless ATC authorizes otherwise.
SFRA.definition: Airspace of defined dimensions, above land areas or territorial waters. In it, the flight of aircraft obeys 14 CFR part 93, unless ATC authorizes otherwise.
SFRA.note: This type is not in AJP-3.3.5 Annex B. It is an airspace type of civil aviation, thus it is an `airspace_type` value, not a catalogue code.

TRSA.name: Terminal Radar Service Area
TRSA.locator: Entry terminal radar service area, page T-3
TRSA.source_text: Airspace surrounding designated airports wherein ATC provides radar vectoring, sequencing, and separation on a full-time basis for all IFR and participating VFR aircraft. The AIM contains an explanation of TRSA. TRSAs are depicted on VFR aeronautical charts. Pilot participation is urged but is not mandatory.
TRSA.paraphrase: Charted airspace around designated airports where ATC gives full-time radar vectoring, sequencing and separation to IFR and participating VFR aircraft; participation is voluntary, and it is not an airspace class.
TRSA.definition: Airspace around a designated airport. In it, ATC gives radar vectoring, sequencing and separation full time. This service is for all IFR aircraft and participating VFR aircraft. This service is not mandatory for pilots. It is not an airspace class.
TRSA.note: This type is not in AJP-3.3.5 Annex B. It is an airspace type of civil aviation, thus it is an `airspace_type` value, not a catalogue code.

ModeCVeil.name: Mode C Veil
ModeCVeil.source_text: Mode C Veil. The airspace within 30 nautical miles of an airport listed in Appendix D, section 1 of 14 CFR part 91 (generally primary airports within Class B airspace areas), from the surface upward to 10,000 feet MSL. Unless otherwise authorized by ATC, aircraft operating within this airspace must be equipped with an operable radar beacon transponder with automatic altitude reporting capability and operable ADS−B Out equipment.
ModeCVeil.paraphrase: The airspace within 30 nautical miles of a listed primary Class B airport from the surface to 10,000 feet MSL, where aircraft need an altitude-reporting transponder and broadcast position equipment unless ATC authorizes otherwise.
ModeCVeil.definition: The airspace that is 30 nautical miles or less from an airport in Appendix D, section 1 of 14 CFR part 91. It goes from the surface to 10,000 feet above MSL. Unless ATC authorizes a different procedure, aircraft in it have a serviceable transponder with automatic altitude reporting and serviceable `ADS-B Out` equipment.
ModeCVeil.note: Each airport in the list is usually a primary airport in class B airspace. 14 CFR 91.215(b)(2) does not use Mode C veil as a name. This type is not in AJP-3.3.5 Annex B. It is an airspace type of civil aviation, thus it is an `airspace_type` value, not a catalogue code.

RMZ.name: Radio Mandatory Zone
RMZ.locator: Article 2, point 106, consolidated page 13; SERA.6005(a), page 42

references.note: Annex 11 does not define the RMZ.

RMZ.source_text: ‘radio mandatory zone (RMZ)’ means an airspace of defined dimensions wherein the carriage and operation of radio equipment is mandatory;
RMZ.paraphrase: Airspace of defined dimensions where aircraft must carry and operate radio equipment.
RMZ.definition: Airspace of defined dimensions in which the carriage and operation of radio equipment is mandatory.
RMZ.note: ICAO Annex 11 and Annex 2 do not give a definition of this zone. The definition comes from the EU rules of the air. This type is not in AJP-3.3.5 Annex B. It is an airspace type of civil aviation, thus it is an `airspace_type` value, not a catalogue code.

TMZ.name: Transponder Mandatory Zone
TMZ.locator: Article 2, point 136, consolidated page 16; SERA.6005(b), page 42

references.note: States set transponder carriage requirements in defined portions of airspace; Annex 11 does not use the name.

TMZ.source_text: ‘transponder mandatory zone (TMZ)’ means an airspace of defined dimensions wherein the carriage and operation of pressure-altitude reporting transponders is mandatory;
TMZ.paraphrase: Airspace of defined dimensions where aircraft must carry and operate pressure-altitude reporting transponders.
TMZ.definition: Airspace of defined dimensions in which the carriage and operation of a pressure-altitude reporting transponder is mandatory.
TMZ.note: ICAO Annex 11 and Annex 2 do not give a definition of this zone. The definition comes from the EU rules of the air. This type is not in AJP-3.3.5 Annex B. It is an airspace type of civil aviation, thus it is an `airspace_type` value, not a catalogue code.

ClassA.name: ICAO Class A Airspace
ClassA.source_text: Class A. IFR flights only are permitted, all flights are provided with air traffic control service and are separated from each other.
ClassA.paraphrase: IFR flights only; all flights receive ATC service, need an ATC clearance and are separated from each other.
ClassA.definition: Airspace only for IFR flights. All flights get ATC service, and an ATC clearance is necessary. ATC separates all flights from each other.
ClassA.note: Annex 11 Appendix 4 gives the ATC clearance requirement. The catalogue code `CLSA` gives the AJP-3.3.5 text of this class.

ClassB.name: ICAO Class B Airspace
ClassB.source_text: Class B. IFR and VFR flights are permitted, all flights are provided with air traffic control service and are separated from each other.
ClassB.paraphrase: IFR and VFR flights; all flights receive ATC service, need an ATC clearance and are separated from each other.
ClassB.definition: Airspace for IFR and VFR flights. All flights get ATC service, and an ATC clearance is necessary. ATC separates all flights from each other.
ClassB.us_note: In the United States, ATC separates VFR flights with radar. When the radar does not operate, ATC stops this service for VFR flights.
ClassB.note: Annex 11 Appendix 4 gives the ATC clearance requirement. The catalogue code `CLSB` gives the AJP-3.3.5 text of this class.

ClassC.name: ICAO Class C Airspace
ClassC.source_text: Class C. IFR and VFR flights are permitted, all flights are provided with air traffic control service and IFR flights are separated from other IFR flights and from VFR flights. VFR flights are separated from IFR flights and receive traffic information in respect of other VFR flights.
ClassC.paraphrase: IFR and VFR flights; all flights receive ATC service and need an ATC clearance; IFR flights are separated from all flights, VFR flights from IFR flights, and VFR flights receive traffic information on other VFR flights.
ClassC.definition: Airspace for IFR and VFR flights. All flights get ATC service, and an ATC clearance is necessary. ATC separates IFR flights from all other flights, and VFR flights from IFR flights. VFR flights get traffic information about other VFR flights.
ClassC.us_note: In the United States, a VFR flight gets radio contact with ATC before it goes in. An ATC clearance is not necessary.
ClassC.note: Annex 11 Appendix 4 gives the ATC clearance requirement. The catalogue code `CLSC` gives the AJP-3.3.5 text of this class.

ClassD.name: ICAO Class D Airspace
ClassD.source_text: Class D. IFR and VFR flights are permitted and all flights are provided with air traffic control service, IFR flights are separated from other IFR flights and receive traffic information in respect of VFR flights, VFR flights receive traffic information in respect of all other flights.
ClassD.paraphrase: IFR and VFR flights; all flights receive ATC service and need an ATC clearance; IFR flights are separated from IFR flights only and receive traffic information on VFR flights; VFR flights receive traffic information on all other flights.
ClassD.definition: Airspace for IFR and VFR flights. All flights get ATC service, and an ATC clearance is necessary. ATC separates IFR flights only from other IFR flights. IFR flights get traffic information about VFR flights, and VFR flights get traffic information about all other flights.
ClassD.us_note: In the United States, a VFR flight gets radio contact with ATC before it goes in. An ATC clearance is not necessary.
ClassD.note: Annex 11 Appendix 4 gives the ATC clearance requirement. The catalogue code `CLSD` gives the AJP-3.3.5 text of this class.

ClassE.name: ICAO Class E Airspace
ClassE.source_text: Class E. IFR and VFR flights are permitted, IFR flights are provided with air traffic control service and are separated from other IFR flights. All flights receive traffic information as far as is practical. Class E shall not be used for control zones.
ClassE.paraphrase: IFR and VFR flights; only IFR flights receive ATC service, need an ATC clearance and are separated from other IFR flights; all flights receive traffic information as far as practical; not used for control zones.
ClassE.definition: Airspace for IFR and VFR flights. Only IFR flights get ATC service, and an ATC clearance is necessary only for IFR flights. ATC separates IFR flights only from other IFR flights. All flights get traffic information as far as practical. A control zone cannot be class E airspace.
ClassE.note: Annex 11 Appendix 4 gives the ATC clearance requirement. The catalogue code `CLSE` gives the AJP-3.3.5 text of this class.

ClassF.name: ICAO Class F Airspace
ClassF.source_text: Class F. IFR and VFR flights are permitted, all participating IFR flights receive an air traffic advisory service and all flights receive flight information service if requested.
ClassF.paraphrase: IFR and VFR flights; participating IFR flights receive an air traffic advisory service; all flights receive flight information service on request; no ATC clearance.
ClassF.definition: Airspace for IFR and VFR flights. No flight gets ATC service, and an ATC clearance is not necessary. Participating IFR flights get an air traffic advisory service, which separates them from other IFR flights as far as practical. All flights get flight information service when they ask for it.
ClassF.us_note: The United States does not use class F airspace.
ClassF.note: Annex 11 Appendix 4 gives the ATC clearance requirement. The catalogue code `CLSF` gives the AJP-3.3.5 text of this class.

ClassG.name: ICAO Class G Airspace
ClassG.source_text: Class G. IFR and VFR flights are permitted and receive flight information service if requested.
ClassG.paraphrase: IFR and VFR flights; flight information service on request only; no ATC service and no ATC clearance.
ClassG.definition: Airspace for IFR and VFR flights. No flight gets ATC service or separation, and an ATC clearance is not necessary. All flights get flight information service when they ask for it.
ClassG.note: Annex 11 Appendix 4 gives the ATC clearance requirement. The catalogue code `CLSG` gives the AJP-3.3.5 text of this class.

UIR.name: Upper Flight Information Region
UIR.source_text: Where a flight information region is limited by an upper flight information region, the lower limit specified for the upper flight information region shall constitute the upper vertical limit of the flight information region and shall coincide with a VFR cruising level of the tables in Appendix 3 to Annex 2.
UIR.paraphrase: A flight information region above another one; its lower limit is the upper limit of the lower region and a VFR cruising level.
UIR.definition: A FIR above a different FIR. Its floor is the ceiling of the lower FIR and is a VFR cruising level. Its procedures can be different from the procedures of the lower FIR.
UIR.note: Annex 11 Chapter 1 does not give a definition of this region. The definition comes from the rules for its limits in paragraph 2.11.2.

ATZ.name: Aerodrome Traffic Zone
ATZ.source_text: ‘aerodrome traffic zone’ means an airspace of defined dimensions established around an aerodrome for the protection of aerodrome traffic;
ATZ.paraphrase: Airspace of defined dimensions around an aerodrome that protects aerodrome traffic.
ATZ.definition: Airspace of defined dimensions around an aerodrome. Its function is the protection of aerodrome traffic.
ATZ.note: The definition comes from the EU rules of the air.

MOA.name: Military Operations Area
MOA.source_text: A military operations area (MOA) is airspace established outside of Class A airspace to separate or segregate certain non−hazardous military flight activities from IFR aircraft and to identify for VFR aircraft where these activities are conducted.
MOA.paraphrase: Airspace outside Class A that separates non-hazardous military flight activities from IFR traffic and shows VFR pilots where they occur.
MOA.definition: Airspace that is not in class A airspace. It separates flight training of armed forces that is not dangerous from IFR aircraft. It also shows VFR aircraft where this training occurs. When it is active, ATC lets an IFR flight go through it only when ATC can separate the flight.
MOA.note: The FAA puts the MOA in special use airspace without regulatory status. When ATC cannot separate an IFR flight from the training, it changes the route or altitude of the flight.

Alert.name: Alert Area

references.locator: Entry special use airspace, item a, page S-7

Alert.source_text: Alert areas are depicted on aeronautical charts to inform nonparticipating pilots of areas that may contain a high volume of pilot training or an unusual type of aerial activity. Pilots should be particularly alert when flying in these areas. All activity within an alert area must be conducted in accordance with CFRs, without waiver, and pilots of participating aircraft as well as pilots transiting the area must be equally responsible for collision avoidance.
Alert.paraphrase: Charted airspace that may contain much pilot training or unusual aerial activity, not hazardous to aircraft; all pilots share collision avoidance.
Alert.definition: Airspace that can contain a large quantity of pilot training or an unusual type of flight. This training and these flights are not dangerous to aircraft. Charts show the area to tell the pilots of non-participating aircraft about it. All flights in it obey the Code of Federal Regulations. Each pilot in it has the same task of collision avoidance.
Alert.note: The FAA puts the alert area in special use airspace without regulatory status.

Warning.name: Warning Area
Warning.source_text: A warning area is airspace of defined dimensions, extending from three nautical miles outward from the coast of the U.S., that contains activity that may be hazardous to nonparticipating aircraft. The purpose of such warning areas is to warn nonparticipating pilots of the potential danger. A warning area may be located over domestic or international waters or both.
Warning.paraphrase: Airspace of defined dimensions from three nautical miles off the US coast with activity that may be hazardous to nonparticipating aircraft.
Warning.definition: Airspace of known dimensions that starts 3 nautical miles from the coast of the United States. It contains tasks that can be dangerous to non-participating aircraft. Its function is to tell the pilots of non-participating aircraft about this risk. It can be above the waters of the United States, above international waters or above the two.
Warning.note: The FAA puts the warning area in special use airspace without regulatory status.

Sector.name: Control Sector
Sector.locator: Entry control sector, pages C-8 and C-9
Sector.source_text: An airspace area of defined horizontal and vertical dimensions for which a controller or group of controllers has air traffic control responsibility, normally within an air route traffic control center or an approach control facility. Sectors are established based on predominant traffic flows, altitude strata, and controller workload. Pilot communications during operations within a sector are normally maintained on discrete frequencies assigned to the sector.
Sector.paraphrase: Airspace of defined horizontal and vertical dimensions for which a controller or group of controllers has ATC responsibility.
Sector.definition: Airspace of known horizontal and vertical dimensions. One controller or a group of controllers controls the air traffic in it. The primary traffic flows, the altitude layers and the work of the controllers set its limits. Pilots in it usually speak to ATC on the frequencies of the sector.
Sector.note: A sector is usually in an en-route centre or an approach control facility.
